tasks.scenario: You investigate the log processing script Meera mentioned. It uses s3fs-fuse to mount an S3 bucket directly as a local filesystem path (/mnt/s3-logs/), and the script treats it exactly like a local disk — opening files, appending log lines, renaming rotated log files, and listing directory contents.
tasks.question: Before diagnosing anything specific, what's the most important thing to understand about this setup?
options: A) S3 IS actually a real filesystem underneath, so this approach should work exactly like a local disk with no meaningful difference

B) S3 is fundamentally a key-value object store, not a filesystem — s3fs-fuse is a translation layer that makes it LOOK like a filesystem to the script, but every filesystem-like operation (append, rename, list) gets translated into one or more actual S3 API calls behind the scenes, each with its own cost and latency
C) This setup is fine because s3fs-fuse eliminates all S3 API calls entirely, making it functionally identical to a local disk
D) The only issue is naming — the mount path should be renamed to something clearer, otherwise this approach is architecturally sound
tasks.explanation: S3 fundamentally key-value store — object store, filesystem not. s3fs-fuse a translation layer, for script filesystem like feel does, but each operation (append, rename, list) real S3 API call-a translate will happen, cost and latency real-a will be. This first understand must do needed point.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — S3 object store, filesystem not. s3fs-fuse just a translation layer, real API calls behind it.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — S3 real filesystem not. s3fs-fuse translation layer only, actual API calls happen behind the scenes.

tasks.question: On a real filesystem, renaming a file is typically a cheap, near-instant metadata operation. What actually happens when you 'rename' an object in S3?
options: A) S3 has a true, native rename operation that works exactly like a filesystem, updating only metadata with no data movement

C) S3 objects can never be renamed under any circumstances, only deleted and manually re-uploaded
D) Renaming only works for objects smaller than 1KB

tasks.scenario: You dig into exactly what the log script does through its s3fs-fuse mount, over a typical day.
tasks.broken_config:
Log script behavior (via /mnt/s3-logs/ s3fs-fuse mount):
├── Appends a new line to the current log file roughly every 2 seconds (each append triggers a full re-upload of the object under s3fs-fuse's default behavior, since S3 has no true append operation either)
├── "Renames" the log file at each hourly rotation (a COPY + DELETE per rotation, 24 times/day)
├── Lists the "directory" contents before each rotation to check for existing files (a LIST API call, potentially expensive at scale)
└── Estimated actual S3 API calls per day: ~43,200 PUT-equivalent calls (from appends) + 48 COPY/DELETE calls (from rotations) + 24 LIST calls

S3 request pricing: PUT/COPY requests ~₹0.0004 each, LIST requests ~₹0.0004 each, GET requests ~₹0.00008 each
what_to_find: The append-every-2-seconds pattern is the biggest issue — S3 has no true append operation, so s3fs-fuse likely re-uploads the ENTIRE current log file on every single append, meaning a growing file gets re-uploaded in full, over and over, all day

This means write costs scale with (file size × number of appends), not just the actual amount of new data being written — a massive inefficiency compared to just writing to a local file and uploading complete files periodically
The hourly rename operations, while smaller in count, are also unnecessary S3 API cost that a native upload pattern (write locally, upload once per rotation) would avoid entirely

At roughly ₹0.0004 per PUT-equivalent call, ~43,200 calls/day is already about ₹17.28/day just from this one script's append pattern alone — and this is likely only ONE of several similar scripts across the fleet
tasks.correct_fix: Rewrite the log script to write to a local file normally (no S3 mount at all), and use the S3 SDK/CLI to upload the completed log file to S3 once per rotation (e.g., hourly), rather than mounting S3 as a filesystem and letting every local-style operation translate into a real API call.
tasks.explanation: This exact spec mistake — S3-a mounted drive like use doing, real cost implications-a purinjikaama. Local-first, batch-upload approach real fix — S3's actual model (key-value, batch operations) respect doing.

Run the new version in parallel with the old one for a short period, comparing output to confirm equivalent behavior
Once confirmed equivalent, cut over fully to the new version and unmount the s3fs-fuse mount
Monitor the next billing cycle to confirm the expected reduction in S3 request costs

cases.case_1: Storing product images that customers view via the app, accessed frequently from anywhere, no filesystem semantics needed
cases.case_2: The root volume of an EC2 instance running a database, needing genuine filesystem behavior and low-latency block-level access
cases.case_3: A shared directory that THREE different EC2 instances need to read and write simultaneously, with real file-locking semantics
cases.case_4: Long-term archival of old order records for compliance, rarely accessed, cost being the primary concern
cases.case_5: A single instance's temporary scratch space for a batch job, needing fast local disk access with no sharing requirement

correct_answers.case_1: S3 — object storage fits perfectly for frequently-accessed, app-served files with no filesystem semantics needed
correct_answers.case_2: EBS — block storage attached to one instance, true filesystem semantics, low latency, exactly what a database root volume needs
correct_answers.case_3: EFS — the ONLY one of these three that supports genuine multi-instance shared filesystem access with real file-locking
correct_answers.case_4: S3 (with a lifecycle policy to a cheaper storage class like Glacier) — archival, cost-focused, rarely-accessed data is S3's strength, especially with tiering
correct_answers.case_5: EBS (or even instance store if truly ephemeral) — single-instance, fast, local, no sharing needed, doesn't need EFS's shared-access overhead or S3's object model
